problem: Social navigation policies are hard to evaluate: simulation cannot realistically model human behavior, while in-the-wild studies are unrepeatable, costly and confounded by many uncontrolled variables. There is no shared, comparable benchmark.
motivation: Progress in socially compliant navigation needs shared, realistic, repeatable and scalable benchmarks. Reducing interactions to canonical scenarios with lightweight specifications lets different labs replicate them, and in-situ human ratings capture social expectations that ex-situ observers or geometric metrics miss.
key_idea: Define five canonical, lightweight real-world social navigation scenarios (each in two locations) and score policies with a per-scenario Likert questionnaire that participants answer immediately after each run.
insight: Questionnaire scores were consistent across locations, across three participants (SAVG 2.5/2.7/2.8), and across 90 repeated runs on different dates. Batches of about 30 runs already give stable estimates. The metric also separated MPC (SAVG 2.2) from MPC+BC (4.3) in frontal approach. In-situ ratings also caught a brief foot collision that an external observer would hardly notice.
method: Canonical scenarios: five scenarios (frontal approach, intersection wait, intersection gesture, narrow doorway, blind corner), each specified only by robot start/end points and a short human instruction, with no constraints on environment or human appearance.
Two instantiations: each scenario is set up at two locations in the building (e.g. F1/F2) to test repeatability across physical spaces.
In-situ questionnaire metric: 4-5 statements per scenario rated on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = cannot tell), asked immediately after each run; negatively worded items are reverse coded.
Aggregate scores: per-question average (QAVG), per-scenario average (SAVG) and standard deviation.
Validation protocol: reliability is tested with 10 runs per scenario and location, 3 participants, 90 runs by one participant, and two policies compared.
Test policies: an iLQR-based MPC baseline versus MPC plus a behavioral-cloning CNN that predicts waypoints, trained on 300 expert trajectories for frontal approach.

setting.backbone: iLQR-based MPC controller (baseline); CNN waypoint predictor with MPC (BC policy)
setting.training_data: 300 expert trajectories of the frontal approach scenario for the BC policy; MPC needs no training
setting.observation: real robot onboard sensing (not detailed); human ratings by questionnaire
setting.action_space: linear and angular velocity commands (MPC); waypoints predicted by CNN for the MPC
setting.privileged: none (the robot was manually controlled by an operator when enacting scenario definitions)

numbers_note: Scores are questionnaire averages per scenario (not standard navigation metrics). Only a few representative rows are listed; Table II also gives SAVG for the other scenarios/locations (e.g. W1 2.1, W2 1.3, G1 2.6, G2 2.1, N1 1.9, N2 1.7, B1 3.1, B2 2.7).
results: The MPC policy gets SAVG between 1.3 and 3.1 across the five scenarios and two locations, with consistent ratings across locations, participants and repeated runs. On frontal approach, the MPC+BC policy scores 4.3 versus 2.2 for plain MPC, showing the metric can tell policies apart.
limitations: Only a pilot study with one robot, one building and a simple MPC baseline plus one BC policy tested on a single scenario
Scenarios focus on passive/yielding robot behavior and the Likert questionnaire is subjective, with few participants (one participant for 90 runs, three for the bias test)
Requires physical robot and human enactors, which limits scalability compared with simulation
